_comment: Storyboard for the Grade 2 Mathematics unit lecture film, How Much, How Long. Rendered by tools/create-ehel-unit-lecture.js. See lecture-video/BRIEF.md. Every beat is one narration clip; art.at names the phrases a picture waits for, and the page refuses to load if a phrase is not in its beat's say. The chapters follow the lesson's own steps in order - longer and shorter, measure with cubes, reading a ruler and drawing a line, which unit, the balance and the jug, and a scale read between its marks - in the lesson's own numbers: the pencil 7 cubes long, the same pencil ending at the 8, a line drawn to the 6, a longer pencil about 15 cm and a door about 2 m, the apple balanced by 100 g and 200 g at 300 g, the jug poured three times to 300 ml, and the ribbon on the halfway mark between 30 and 40 at 35 cm.
title: How Much, How Long
subtitle: Grade 2 Mathematics
objectives: Understand that length is a fixed distance between two points. Estimate and measure lengths using non-standard or standard units.
Draw and measure lines, using standard units.
Understand that mass is the quantity of matter in an object. Estimate and measure familiar objects using non-standard or standard units.
Understand that capacity is the maximum amount that an object can contain. Estimate and measure the capacity of familiar objects using non-standard or standard units.
Understand a measuring scale as a continuous number line where intermediate points have value.

beats.say: Some things are long. Some things are heavy. Some hold a lot.
Measuring tells you exactly how long, how heavy, or how much.
Here are a pencil and a crayon. Which one is longer?
They both start in the same place, on the same line.
Now look at where each one ends. The pencil ends further along.
So the pencil is longer, and the crayon is shorter.
A fat thing is not a long thing. Only the length along it counts.
You can measure with cubes. Lay them along the pencil, with no gaps.
Then count them: one, two, three, four, five, six, seven.
The pencil is seven cubes long. Cubes are the unit here.
Every cube must be the same size, or the count means nothing.
A ruler measures in centimetres. The marks are all the same size.
Line up the end of the pencil with the 0, not with the 1.
Read the number where the pencil ends. It ends at the 8.
So the pencil is 8 centimetres long. You measured it.
To draw a line 6 centimetres long, start at 0 and stop at the 6.
Now choose a unit that fits. A longer pencil is about 15 centimetres.
A door is about 2 metres tall. Big things need metres.
An apple is light, so grams. A school bag is heavy, so kilograms.
A spoon of medicine is millilitres. A bath of water is litres.
Mass is how heavy a thing is. A balance can find it.
The apple side tips down, so the apple is the heavier side.
Add 100 grams, then 200 grams. Now the beam is level.
Level means both sides match. The apple is 300 grams.
Capacity is how much a jug holds. Each mark is 100 millilitres.
Pour in three times, and the water reaches the 300 mark.
A measuring scale is a number line, and not every mark has a number.
Here the numbered marks say 30 and 40.
One small mark sits halfway between them. It is worth 5 more.
The ribbon ends on that mark, so it is 35 centimetres long.
Start at 0, use one unit all the way, and read where it ends.
Small things take small units. Big things take big ones.
A balance finds mass, a jug finds capacity, and every mark counts.
